item.title: New Zealand services sector grows for four months straight as PSI holds at 50.9
item.description:
A reading barely above 50 does little to shift the outlook for the New Zealand dollar, which takes its lead from global risk sentiment and rate expectations more than from second-tier surveys. A soft employment component and persistent concern over interest rates point to an economy still sensitive to borrowing costs, which supports the case for the Reserve Bank of New Zealand to stay cautious. The gap between strong manufacturing and sluggish services also suggests the recovery is not yet broad enough to drive domestic inflation. Election uncertainty is likely to keep local data in this subdued range until the result is known.

--

New Zealand’s services sector is growing again, but only just, as businesses keep their wallets shut until voters have had their say.

Summary:

  • The BNZ-BusinessNZ Performance of Services Index was 50.9 in September, from 51.0 in August and 50.5 in July
  • It’s the fourth consecutive month of expansion, following two years of contraction
  • New orders (52.6) and inventories (52.3) were the strongest components; supplier deliveries (49.4) and employment (49.8) were below 50
  • Around 60% of respondent comments were negative, little changed from August
  • Cost of living, fuel prices, interest rates and election uncertainty dominate business concerns
  • Services growth continues to lag manufacturing, which has been well above 50 for some time

New Zealand’s services sector expanded for a fourth straight month in September, though only modestly, according to the BNZ-BusinessNZ Performance of Services Index (PSI), with businesses holding back ahead of the general election.

The index registered 50.9, fractionally below August’s 51.0 but above July’s 50.5. A reading above 50 indicates expansion and below 50 contraction, so the sector remains in growth territory, but only just.

The four-month run marks a meaningful turnaround after two years in which the index sat in contraction. The pace of growth, however, remains subdued, and it continues to lag well behind manufacturing, where the equivalent Performance of Manufacturing Index has held comfortably above 50 for some time, economists noted.

Beneath the headline, the picture was uneven. New orders and inventories were the strongest components, at 52.6 and 52.3 respectively, pointing to some forward momentum in demand. Supplier deliveries were the weakest at 49.4, and employment also sat just below 50 at 49.8, a sign that firms are not yet confident enough to add staff and that the recovery remains narrowly based.

Business sentiment was little changed from August, with around 60% of respondents’ comments negative. Cost of living pressures, fuel prices, interest rates and uncertainty around the election were the dominant concerns.

BusinessNZ chief executive Katherine Rich described four consecutive months above the breakeven line as an encouraging run despite the slight easing in September. She said caution remained deeply embedded across the sector, with many businesses adopting a wait-and-see stance ahead of the election, and suggested that hesitancy was likely to cap any stronger pickup until the political outlook becomes clearer.

The result leaves the services sector on a fragile footing. With the election approaching, the coming months will show whether firms’ caution lifts once the outcome is known, or whether cost pressures and high borrowing costs continue to restrain the recovery regardless of who forms the next government.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Euro slides against Australian dollar as three European headwinds hit early trade
item.description:
The drop in EUR/AUD is a euro story first, which makes it vulnerable to a partial reversal once main Asian centres open and liquidity improves. The real test comes with the European open: French government bond spreads over Bunds and the euro’s performance against the US dollar will show whether the weekend headlines are being priced as a lasting political and fiscal risk or as a passing shock. Tuesday’s NATO council meeting is a further event risk for the euro. On the Australian side, Kent’s remarks offer the only scheduled domestic catalyst, and anything read as dovish would blunt the Aussie’s gains.

---

Earlier:

  • EUR update, France riots: 2,400 arrested as cost-of-living protests turn to looting and arson
  • US threatens EU with devastating retaliation if Brussels curbs Starlink spectrum access
  • Romanian F-16s shoot down two drones over Black Sea, NATO council to meet Tuesday

---

The Australian dollar is winning against the euro mostly by default, as Europe brings riots, drones and a trade threat to the Monday open.

Summary:

  • EUR/AUD is lower in very early Asia-Pacific trade, with flows moving out of the euro and into the Australian dollar
  • French riots over the weekend, with around 2,400 arrests, are the main weight on the euro
  • Romanian jets shooting down two drones over the Black Sea adds regional security risk, with NATO to meet on Tuesday
  • A US warning of retaliation if the EU curbs Starlink’s spectrum access adds transatlantic trade friction
  • There is little fresh Australian news, and liquidity is thin with Australian trade getting underway with earlieer trade taking place when only New Zealand was open
  • RBA Assistant Governor Christopher Kent speaks at 23:05 GMT Sunday, 19:05 US Eastern (10:05 AEDT Monday)

The euro has opened the week on the back foot against the Australian dollar, with EUR/AUD sliding in very early Asia-Pacific trade as three separate European headlines from the weekend combined to sour sentiment toward the single currency.

The biggest weight is France. A nationwide day of protest over fuel prices, wages and public services on Saturday descended into rioting, looting and arson in cities from Paris to Marseille and Limoges, with around 2,400 arrests and close to 1,000 police officers injured. President Emmanuel Macron condemned the violence but stopped short of declaring a state of emergency. For currency markets, the concern is less the damage itself than what it signals: deep social discontent in the euro area’s second-largest economy, a government with limited fiscal room to respond, and a presidential election in 2027 that the unrest has already begun to shape.

Security risk on the bloc’s eastern edge is the second factor. Romanian F-16s shot down two drones over the country’s Black Sea waters on Saturday, days after drones struck two chemical tankers off its coast. The drones’ origin has not been disclosed, and NATO allies are due to discuss the incidents at a North Atlantic Council meeting on Tuesday.

Third, transatlantic trade friction has resurfaced. The US ambassador to the EU warned European companies could face severe retaliation in the American market if Brussels presses ahead with a plan to reserve part of its satellite-to-smartphone spectrum for European operators, a move that would curb access for SpaceX’s Starlink.

There is little fresh, Australia-specific news behind the move, and it looks driven by the euro side of the cross. Early flows have favoured the Australian dollar at the euro’s expense, though with New Zealand effectively the only major centre open, liquidity is thin and early price action may exaggerate the underlying shift.

The first domestic event of note is a fireside chat with Reserve Bank of Australia Assistant Governor (Financial Markets) Christopher Kent at the Commonwealth Bank’s Global Markets Conference in Sydney, scheduled for 23:05 GMT on Sunday, 19:05 US Eastern (10:05 AEDT on Monday). Any remarks touching on the policy outlook or currency conditions would give the Australian dollar its own driver, rather than leaving it to trade purely as the beneficiary of European weakness.

item.title: EUR update, France riots: 2,400 arrested as cost-of-living protests turn to looting and arson
item.description:
The unrest adds a domestic political risk layer to the euro, which was already softer in early Asia-Pacific trade, and to French government bonds, where investors are sensitive to anything that pressures spending. Street pressure for more public investment collides with France’s high debt and deficit, so the spread of French yields over German Bunds is the clearest gauge of whether markets see a fiscal or political cost. Retail and luxury names with heavy French store footprints face direct damage and insurance costs, plus the risk of weaker footfall if disruption persists. A revival of yellow vest-style protests would extend these risks well beyond a single weekend.

---

Earlier EU news, multiple weight on the euro this morning here early:

  • US threatens EU with devastating retaliation if Brussels curbs Starlink spectrum access
  • Romanian F-16s shoot down two drones over Black Sea, NATO council to meet Tuesday

---

A peaceful national day of protest over living costs was hijacked by rioters, leaving France with record arrests, a gutted town hall and a government with little fiscal room to answer the anger behind it.

Summary:

  • Around 2,400 people were arrested and close to 1,000 police officers injured after protests across France turned violent on Saturday
  • More than 550,000 people marched over fuel prices, wages and public services, per the interior ministry; the CGT union estimated 800,000
  • Rioters torched Limoges town hall, burned Lyon’s tourist office and looted shops in Paris, Marseille, Lille and other cities
  • One protester died of cardiac arrest; Carrefour said 50 stores were damaged, with losses in the tens of millions of euros
  • Macron condemned the violence and refused a state of emergency, but said prefects could ban protests where needed
  • The unrest is feeding into the 2027 presidential race, with government spending constrained by high debt

France is counting the cost of one of its most violent days of unrest in years after nationwide protests over living costs and failing public services gave way to rioting, looting and arson in cities across the country on Saturday, leaving around 2,400 people under arrest and close to 1,000 police officers injured, according to Interior Minister Laurent Nunez.

More than half a million people marched, by the interior ministry’s count, with the CGT union putting turnout nearer 800,000. Most demonstrated peacefully, voicing anger over fuel prices, low wages and the state of schools, as a month-long student movement merged with wider social discontent. Violent groups, many masked, broke away to attack public buildings, ransack shops and confront police, who responded with tear gas, batons and water cannon.

The damage was widespread. In Limoges, rioters set fire to the town hall, a building more than a century old, and its clock tower collapsed in the blaze; local officials said much of it was lost. Lyon’s tourist office was burned, a masked group forced its way into the prefect’s residence in Bordeaux, and protesters broke into Marseille city hall. In Paris, luxury boutiques, supermarkets, bakeries and wine shops were smashed or emptied. Paris police said arrests in the capital alone, at more than 850, were a record.

The human toll extended beyond the police. One protester died after a cardiac arrest in Paris, and Le Figaro reported that a teenager in Saint-Etienne lost a hand to a police grenade. Fresh clashes flared in Paris and Marseille on Sunday, Reuters reported.

Carrefour chief executive Alexandre Bompard said 50 of the retailer’s stores were damaged, 20 of them looted, with losses in the tens of millions of euros. Economy Minister Roland Lescure promised support for affected businesses.

In a televised address, President Emmanuel Macron condemned the violence, saying it could not be justified, while drawing a line between peaceful protesters with legitimate grievances and those bent on destruction. He declined calls from some on the right to declare a state of emergency, but said prefects would be able to ban protests where needed to protect public buildings and businesses, and promised transparency on the police response. The government has blamed ultra-left groups and opportunistic criminals.

The unrest has quickly become a campaign issue ahead of the 2027 presidential election. National Rally leader Marine Le Pen called for calm and accused the hard left of legitimising the violence, while France Unbowed’s Jean-Luc Melenchon, who backed the protests, distanced himself from the looting and urged Macron to address students’ demands.

The next test is whether calls online to revive the yellow vest movement gain traction. With high debt and a large deficit limiting room for new spending, the government has little fiscal scope to buy calm.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: US threatens EU with devastating retaliation if Brussels curbs Starlink spectrum access
item.description:
The warning adds a fresh transatlantic trade risk to a market that had largely treated EU digital regulation as a compliance issue rather than a trigger for US countermeasures. European exporters with heavy US revenue exposure are the most obvious channel if rhetoric turns into action, while EU satellite and telecom operators that would benefit from reserved spectrum now face a more contested path to that advantage. For the euro, a renewed tit-for-tat narrative is a modest headwind at the margin, though nothing concrete has been announced. Investors will look for whether Washington links tech regulation to broader tariff policy, which would raise the stakes well beyond the satellite sector.

---

Earlier:

  • Romanian F-16s shoot down two drones over Black Sea, NATO council to meet Tuesday
  • Monday open indicative forex prices, 19 October 2026

---

Washington is signalling that Europe’s quest for tech independence, from satellite airwaves to cloud rules and big-tech fines, could come with a bill payable in the American market.

Summary:

  • US ambassador to the EU Andrew Puzder warned European companies could face severe retaliation in the US market if Brussels limits American rivals’ access to parts of the EU market, Financial Times (gated) reports
  • The trigger is a Commission proposal to reserve some direct satellite-to-smartphone spectrum for European operators, curbing access for US and Chinese firms including SpaceX’s Starlink
  • SpaceX has warned the plan could weaken connectivity in Ukraine, where Starlink supports civilian and military communications
  • Puzder also criticised the proposed Cloud and AI Development Act and questioned whether Digital Markets Act fines are about competition or revenue
  • He urged the EU to cooperate with the US against China on AI and quantum computing rather than restrict US firms
  • The Commission says its proposal diversifies EU suppliers while staying open to non-EU operators

Washington’s envoy to the European Union has put Brussels on notice that European businesses could pay a heavy price in the American market if the bloc moves to shut US satellite operators out of part of its airwaves, sharpening a transatlantic dispute over who controls Europe’s critical technology.

The flashpoint is a European Commission proposal, tabled this year, to set aside a slice of the spectrum used for direct satellite-to-smartphone connections for European operators. That would shrink the frequencies available to American and Chinese providers, including SpaceX and its Starlink network.

Andrew Puzder, the US ambassador to the EU, told the Financial Times that European firms should be alert to the possibility of retaliation, and suggested the consequences would be severe given how much those companies depend on access to the large US market.

He accepted that Europe has a legitimate interest in safeguarding sensitive government data, but argued that rules designed to weaken American competitors in order to lift domestic ones would not make European industry stronger. US products in the sector were reliable and trusted, he said, adding that Europe did not need what he called “synchronised mediocrity”.

SpaceX has already objected strongly to the spectrum plan, warning that it could degrade connectivity in Ukraine, where Starlink has carried both civilian and military communications since Russia launched its full-scale invasion.

The proposal sits within a wider European drive for technological sovereignty, as policymakers look to reduce reliance on US technology amid concern over the unpredictability of President Donald Trump and the risks of foreign control over critical infrastructure. The Commission has also put forward a Cloud and AI Development Act that would set sovereignty conditions for providers of sensitive cloud services while helping European firms grow into alternatives to US groups.

Puzder also questioned the EU’s enforcement of the Digital Markets Act, asking whether multibillion-euro fines on American technology companies were really about competition or about raising revenue for Europe. He argued that the regulatory approach risked deterring US investment and undermining Europe’s own tech ambitions.

Rather than trying to rein in American firms, he said, Washington and Brussels should cooperate to stay ahead of China in artificial intelligence and quantum computing, echoing Trump’s view that losing that contest would be the worst outcome.

The Commission, for its part, has defended the spectrum proposal, saying it encourages new entrants and more diverse EU suppliers while remaining open to operators from outside the bloc. How Brussels proceeds with the plan, and with its wider sovereignty agenda, will now be watched for signs of whether this dispute moves from rhetoric toward trade measures.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Romanian F-16s shoot down two drones over Black Sea, NATO council to meet Tuesday
item.description:
The euro is lower in early Asia-Pacific trade, though liquidity is very thin with New Zealand effectively the only FX market open, so early moves may overstate conviction. A fresh airspace violation on NATO’s eastern flank adds a geopolitical risk premium to the single currency, and escalating riots in France and elsewhere in the EU are also weighing on the euro. For energy and freight markets, back-to-back drone incidents near Romania’s coast raise the risk of higher war-risk insurance costs and caution among operators using western Black Sea routes. Tuesday’s NATO council meeting is the next catalyst: a firmer collective response could extend risk aversion, while an outcome framed as containment may let the euro stabilise once deeper liquidity returns.

---

EUR marked lower:

  • Monday open indicative forex prices, 19 October 2026

---

Romania has now had to put fighter jets in the air to protect its own Black Sea airspace, turning a regional shipping threat into an issue NATO will take up on Tuesday.

Summary:

  • Romanian Air Force F-16s shot down two drones over Romanian territorial waters in the Black Sea on Saturday, the Defence Ministry said
  • The intercepts took place about 20 km southeast of Sulina; the first drone was downed within two minutes of entering airspace at 14:59 GMT, the second at 15:05 GMT
  • The drones’ country of origin has not been disclosed
  • The incident follows drone strikes on two chemical tankers near Romania’s coast earlier in the week
  • Foreign Minister Oana Toiu said the issue will be raised at a North Atlantic Council meeting on Tuesday
  • The euro is softer in thin early Asian trade, with riots in France and elsewhere in the EU adding pressure

Romanian Air Force F-16 fighter jets shot down two drones over the country’s Black Sea territorial waters on Saturday, the Romanian Defence Ministry said, the latest sign that the security risks around the region’s sea lanes are spilling directly into NATO airspace.

Defence Minister Radu Miruta said on Facebook that Romanian military pilots engaged and destroyed both drones shortly after they illegally entered national airspace. The intercepts took place roughly 20 kilometres southeast of Sulina, according to a report by DW, which drew on AFP and Reuters.

Miruta gave a precise timeline. The first drone crossed into Romanian airspace at 14:59 GMT (10:59 a.m. US Eastern) and was brought down within two minutes. The second was shot down at 15:05 GMT (11:05 a.m. US Eastern), about five minutes after it entered.

Authorities have not said where the drones came from, and no country has been identified as responsible. That gap matters: until the origin is established, the incident remains a confirmed airspace violation rather than an attributed act, and any read on intent or escalation is speculative.

The shootdowns follow an incident earlier in the week in which two chemical tankers were struck by drones near Romania’s Black Sea coast. Taken together, the two episodes point to a growing threat to commercial traffic and to the airspace of a NATO member state in the same stretch of water.

Foreign Minister Oana Toiu pledged on X that the Black Sea would be made safe again, and said the matter will be raised at a meeting of the North Atlantic Council, NATO’s main political decision-making body, on Tuesday.

That meeting is now the key event to watch. Allies’ response will signal whether the incidents are treated as isolated violations or as part of a pattern requiring a stronger collective posture in the Black Sea, with implications for regional shipping, insurance costs and broader European risk sentiment.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: S&P 500 analysis and forecast after the "AI bubble" panic
item.description:
S&P 500 forecast after the AI bubble panic: Why Friday's selloff is not yet a major bearish reversal

Friday's selloff in AI and chip stocks looked alarming, but the S&P 500 E-mini futures (ES) are telling a somewhat less frightening story. Following the October 16 close, my four-hour technical analysis still shows a decline within a broader trading range, rather than a confirmed major bearish trend reversal. The next important test is around 7,668, and I explain why in my video below:

AI stocks were hit hard, but the broader market tells a different story

For investors holding semiconductor and AI-related stocks, Friday was certainly an uncomfortable day.

As Adam Button reported in AI names fall as the Nasdaq comes under fresh pressure, selling extended beyond chipmakers into AI infrastructure, cloud computing and cybersecurity companies. Some individual stocks suffered much steeper losses than the broader equity indices.

The investingLive Americas market wrap showed the Nasdaq down approximately 2.3% on Friday, compared with a 1.2% decline in the S&P 500.

That difference is worth paying attention to.

A sharp decline in popular technology stocks can create the impression that the entire stock market is entering a major collapse. However, weakness in market leaders does not necessarily mean that the broader market has already confirmed a bearish reversal.

We also saw a different picture internationally. European stocks finished higher on Friday and posted weekly gains, illustrating how unevenly the selling pressure was distributed.

This does not make the risks in AI stocks disappear. It simply suggests that we should distinguish between a sharp sector selloff and a confirmed breakdown in the broader stock market.

And that brings me to the S&P 500 chart.

Watch my S&P 500 futures technical analysis and forecast in the video below. I explain the trading range, the price channel and the conditions that would make me considerably more bearish.

Why the S&P 500 still looks like a trading range

The central observation in my analysis is that ES remains within a recognizable trading range.

On the four-hour chart, price has been moving through alternating advances and declines, with sellers taking control near resistance and buyers responding around support.

I also identify a price channel that has helped frame these movements since September. The channel's boundaries and midpoint have repeatedly interacted with price, including around the latest decline.

In particular, the recent selling followed a rejection near two overlapping resistance references: the channel's midpoint and the upper boundary of the range's value area.

The value area is the price region where roughly 70% of the trading volume occurred over the period being examined. Its upper and lower boundaries can help identify where the market has previously accepted substantial trading activity.

After failing near resistance, ES moved back toward the lower boundary of that value area.

This brings us to an especially interesting part of Friday's price action.

S&P 500 futures: Why 7,668 matters

Around 7,668, several technical references come together.

First, this is approximately the lower boundary of the value area for the range examined in the video.

Second, the October 16 decline approached the lower boundary of the price channel.

Third, the market was revisiting a support region associated with earlier lows around September 18 and October 1.

These are three different reasons why traders might pay attention to approximately the same area.

For example, some short sellers may decide to take profits when price reaches established support. Other traders may consider a speculative long position, while traders following the channel could view the lower boundary as an area where a rebound becomes possible.

I am not claiming to know which participants were buying or covering shorts on Friday. The observation is that price reached an area where several recognizable support references converged.

The important point is that Friday's decline had not yet produced the sustained breakdown below this area that I would want to see before interpreting the move as a more significant bearish development.

That does not mean support must hold on the next test. It means the market has not yet provided sufficient evidence for my more bearish scenario.

What would turn the S&P 500 outlook more bearish?

This is where my forecast becomes conditional.

In my opinion, the more meaningful warning would be two or three consecutive completed four-hour candles closing below approximately 7,668.

Why not simply react to the first move below that level?

Because markets frequently cross support or resistance briefly before reversing direction. A momentary break can reflect a liquidity event or a failed attempt to establish a new trading range.

Several consecutive closes below support would provide stronger evidence that sellers are establishing acceptance at lower prices, rather than merely pushing the market temporarily beyond a familiar boundary.

An additional development worth watching would be a subsequent recovery attempt that fails to reclaim the broken support.

For example, if ES breaks below 7,668, rebounds toward that area, encounters renewed selling and then continues lower, the bearish interpretation becomes more credible.

Even then, a downside break would not automatically establish a long-term bear market. It would first signal that the current trading range is potentially resolving lower, with the wider trend requiring further evaluation.

And what if S&P 500 support holds?

The alternative is that buyers continue defending the existing support region.

If ES holds around 7,668 and begins recovering, the next question becomes whether price can reclaim the channel's midpoint and challenge the higher-volume resistance region that previously attracted selling.

Such a recovery would fit the existing trading-range interpretation.

However, I would be careful about declaring a new bullish breakout simply because the market rebounds from support.

There is an important difference between a recovery within a range and a sustained move out of that range.

A rebound could improve the immediate technical picture while leaving the broader market in consolidation.

For now, I am not automatically bullish or bearish. My interpretation is that the recent weakness is meaningful, but the evidence for a major bearish reversal remains incomplete.

The next catalysts: Technology earnings, inflation and the Federal Reserve

Technical support is only part of the picture.

Investors also need to consider what could change market sentiment as trading resumes.

The upcoming earnings calendar could be particularly important for determining whether AI-related selling remains concentrated in certain stocks or spreads further across the market.

As discussed in Earnings week ahead: Banks were upbeat on the economy, now onto tech, the latest bank results suggested that important parts of the US economy remain resilient. The next earnings announcements will provide another opportunity to evaluate how businesses are navigating current conditions.

Meanwhile, inflation, energy prices and monetary policy remain potential sources of volatility.

Giuseppe Dellamotta's review of changing interest-rate expectations illustrates how traders are reassessing the Federal Reserve outlook amid persistent inflation concerns.

One reason this matters for stocks is that higher costs do not necessarily translate into higher corporate profits. Justin Low offers a useful explanation in Why higher inflation doesn't always mean bigger corporate profits.

These macroeconomic concerns also formed part of my earlier Dow Jones futures analysis for October 16, although that analysis reflected an earlier market snapshot before Friday's selling intensified.

Taken together, the question for the coming week is whether disappointing developments cause the broader indices to break established support, or whether the latest weakness remains largely a correction within existing trading structures.

My S&P 500 forecast: Respect the selling, but wait for confirmation

My main takeaway after reviewing Friday's price action is straightforward.

The selling pressure is real, particularly in technology stocks, but the S&P 500 futures chart is not yet confirming the kind of major bearish trend reversal that some investors may fear.

The market has reached an important support region, and the next reaction around 7,668 could provide useful information.

Holding that region would keep the existing trading-range interpretation intact. Sustained four-hour closes below it, particularly followed by a failed recovery, would make me reassess the bearish risks more seriously.

The market could certainly move lower. I am not ruling that out.

But there is a difference between anticipating a major reversal and having sufficient evidence that one is actually developing.

For traders and investors, recognizing that difference can help avoid making decisions based purely on frightening headlines or the latest sharp move in a few popular stocks.

S&P 500 forecast on a wider perspective (the simple weekly chart)

I typically perform some heavy and sophisticated analysis with lots of data but for traders and investors at investingLive.com, I like to simplify and show them the simple charts. Less is more for many of our readers. That is where apx 7600 (shown as 7,608.89 below) comes in, if S&P 500 decides to sell some more. 

S&P 500 futures: The weekly 20 EMA in my above simple chart could become an important support test

S&P 500 E-mini futures (ES) remain in a broader uptrend on the weekly chart, although the latest pullback suggests buyers are facing renewed pressure near the highs.

During the week ending October 16, futures approached the previous week's high near 7,900, but failed to extend the rally. The contract subsequently declined to close around 7,703, a weekly loss of approximately 2.1%.

Despite this weakness, the broader bullish structure has not yet been decisively undermined.

The first area to watch is around 7,670-7,680. The latest weekly low near 7,676 almost matched the late-September low around 7,673, making this an immediate reference area for potential stabilization.

Further below, the 20-week exponential moving average (EMA), currently around 7,609, could become an important support reference if the decline continues.

This moving average has been rising alongside the broader advance. However, price has not yet tested it during the latest pullback, so its ability to attract renewed buying interest remains unproven.

A decline toward the EMA followed by a convincing weekly rebound would support the interpretation that the market is experiencing a correction within a continuing uptrend.

Conversely, a completed weekly close below the moving average, followed by an unsuccessful attempt to recover it, would suggest that the correction may be developing into something more significant. The early-September lows around 7,575-7,585 provide another nearby structural reference.

On the upside, a sustained recovery toward 7,850-7,900 would help restore the bullish case.

The takeaway: The weekly 20 EMA offers a potentially useful future support test, but the more important evidence will be how prices behave if they reach it. A moving average identifies an area worth watching, not a guarantee that buyers will defend it.

This analysis reflects the October 16, 2026 market close and is my technical interpretation as of October 17. It is educational commentary, not financial advice.

This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Oil prices surge higher into the weekend
item.description:
It will be another weekend of pain at the fuel pumps.

WTI crude oil is finishing the week at the highest since September 21 and back over $100 per barrel. WTI last trade up $3.33 to $101.30. Brent crude also touched $110 for the first time since May.

The strong rally to $101 from $98 in the final hours of trading today suggsets lingering worries about US attacks on Iran, particularly after all the news floated this week about the US military preparing MOAB attacks. Trump himself didn't push back against the reports when given the opportunity but he also previously wrote that the US won't attack Iran before the midterms. 

At the same time, things aren't looking great for Republicans in the polls and today the White House announced that new press secretary Katie Zacharia was asked to step down after just five days. We also learned today the US 2026 fiscal year deficit was the highest in five years. Trump may see fresh attacks as a Hail Mary opportunity to try to change the narrative around the war and inflation. 

Alternatively, Iran could try to escalate in order to further drive up oil prices and exact a toll on global consumers in order to gain leverage. 

In any case, there is no real catalyst in the news for today's big gain in oil. What it's doing is reverberating back into stock and bond markets and driving one of the worst days of the year in the Nasdaq, which was last down 2.2%.

Technically, WTI faces resistance at the September high of $106.75 with some breathing room before then. The war high was $119.48 in early March, though the high close was $112.95 as some of the days during the war were extremely volatile.

If nothing happens in the next couple weeks in oil, the focus will turn towards the post-midterms landscape. item.title: US fiscal 2026 budget deficit was the largest in five years
item.description:
• September 2025 was a $198B surplus
  • Outlays $585B vs $346B a year ago
  • Receipts $558B vs $544B a year ago
  • FY2026 deficit $1.992 trillion vs $1.775T in FY2025, the largest in five years
  • FY2026 gross interest on the debt: record $1.36T, up $144B (12%)

Interest is now the main driver of the deficit. The $144B rise in interest costs accounts for about two-thirds of the $217B increase in the full-year shortfall. Treasury will keep rolling debt at higher rates while the Fed is debating hikes rather than cuts, so that line has nowhere to go but up.

The customs numbers are the most interesting part of the release. Gross customs receipts were $25.27B, roughly in line with the recent run rate. But refunds of $19.36B ate up 77% of that, leaving net customs receipts of just $5.91B.

The monthly swing from a $198B surplus to a $27B deficit is mostly about outlays, which jumped $239B y/y while receipts rose only 2.6%. Year-ago September comparisons are notoriously noisy because of payment timing, so the full-year number is the one that matters.

In any case, the headline tells most of the story as the US is in a huge fiscal hole and these are the good times for growth right now. There are going to be some very ugly days ahead and there's no way to grow out of it.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Flying car. Grounded stock. The technicals are not leaning to a "take-off" for Tesla stock
item.description:
The flying car gets attention. But is it good for business?

Tesla’s flying car has certainly brought out the “oohs” and “aahs.” And why not? A car that can briefly take flight is going to get attention. From a marketing perspective, that is a win for Tesla. It gets people talking and gives Elon Musk another opportunity to show what his engineers can do.

But is it good for the business?

That is where I have some questions. How many people need a flying sports car? How much will it cost to develop and produce? Could that money—and engineering talent—be better spent on vehicles that more people can afford and use every day? Will the flying version ever get approved for public use? Or is it simply a gimmick?

I am still waiting for the flux capacitor and the time-machine capability.

Nevertheless, the publicity has value. The payoff for shareholders is less clear.

Elon had his moment. Now the market gets its turn.

Which brings me to the technicals.

Despite all the excitement, the price action helps tell us whether the market is buying the idea—or selling it. And Tesla’s technical picture is not overly bullish.

The car got off the ground. Can the stock do the same?

Let’s look at the levels.

Elon Musk had his moment yesterday. Today, the market gets its turn.

At the open, Tesla shares moved higher, reaching $370.58. However, that high fell just short of the 100-day moving average at $371.13. Buyers had their shot to test that key technical target. They could not get above it.

The price has since rotated lower, reaching $360.20. It is currently trading near $361.50, down about $1 on the day.

Moving averages give sellers something to lean against

In the process, the price also moved back below the near-converged 100- and 200-hour moving averages at $368.85. That gives traders a clear level to watch on any rebound.

Stay below those hourly moving averages, and the sellers retain control. Get above them, and the buyers get another opportunity to challenge the 100-day moving average at $371.13. Getting above—and staying above—that level would strengthen the bullish case.

So far, however, the 100-day moving average has capped the rally, and the hourly moving averages have given way. That does not speak to buyers taking control. It gives the sellers more confidence.

Opinions are one thing. The price action defines the risk.

Now, my questions about the flying car’s viability are simply my thoughts. Others will be more bullish on the idea and excited about a car that can take flight or accelerate from 0 to 60 mph in less than a second.

I still ask: Where exactly are you going to use that? Preferably somewhere without big, fat trees along the side of the road or any cars in sight.

As traders and investors, however, we need to bring the focus back to price. The chart gives us a roadmap. The technical tools help define the risk, the bias and the next targets.

Right now, that roadmap shows Tesla:

  • Below its 100- and 200-hour moving averages near $368.85.

  • Below its 100-day moving average at $371.13.

  • Below its 200-day moving average near $388.02.

What would get the stock off the ground?

There is work to do.

If the stock is going to get off the ground technically, the buyers need to reclaim those moving averages, starting with the hourly levels, and stay above them. Then the 100 day MA and ultimately the 200 day MA at $388.  

Until then, the stock remains grounded, and the sellers remain more in control.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Earnings week ahead: Banks were upbeat on the economy, now onto tech

After market:Robert Half is the sleeper macro report of the week, because temp staffing turns before payrolls do. Weak commentary would undercut the “healthy consumer because healthy jobs” argument. item.title: Bitcoin is little changed on the day, and pushing against a key crossroad. What next?
item.description:
Bitcoin has spent the early part of the week moving back and forth across its 100- and 200-hour moving averages (they are near converged near $82,500). Each modest break above offered an opportunity for the buyers to take control. However, sellers prevailed.  The price moved away from those moving averages and lower, but similarly to the buyers at the high resistance, sellers reached support and found momentum faded as well. And true to form, the price pushed higher. 

Now the price is back at those converged moving averages near $82,500, putting traders at the same key crossroad at the 100 and 200 hour moving averages.

A week of missed opportunities

Bitcoin started the week above its 100-hour moving average and testing its higher 200-hour moving average—the green line on the chart below. Monday’s push briefly cleared that level, but the rally stalled at $84,178. Buyers could not keep the momentum going, and the price reversed below the 100-hour moving average toward swing support between $80,106 and $81,183.

After finding support in that area on Tuesday, buyers took another run to the upside. The rebound carried the price back above both moving averages, shifting the short-term bias in their favor. However, the rally failed to take out Monday’s high at $84,178.

The buyers had their shot. They could not finish the job.

That failure kept sellers in play and they pushed lower. On Wednesday, the price broke below the then-converged moving averages near $83,100, and downside momentum accelerated. By Thursday, bitcoin had fallen through the bottom of the $80,106–$81,183 swing area.

That should have opened the door for further selling. Instead, the break quickly ran out of steam, and the price snapped back above the support zone.

This time, the sellers had their shot. They missed.

Back at the moving-average crossroads

The recovery has now brought bitcoin back to its converged 100- and 200-hour moving averages near $82,500. Those levels are being tested today, and the next move needs follow-through.

For buyers, the job is to get above those moving averages—and stay above them. A sustained break would shift the short-term bias higher and put the following targets in play:

  • $84,178: Monday’s high and the ceiling buyers failed to clear earlier this week.

  • $85,578–$87,374: The higher resistance area containing the September and October cycle highs.

For sellers, the job is to keep a lid on the price at the moving averages. If they can do that and push the price lower, the focus returns to:

  • $81,183–$80,106: The swing support area that has been central to this week’s trading.

  • $76,052: The 38.2% retracement of the rally from the July low to the September high, if support gives way and sellers sustain the break.

The trading lesson: A break needs staying power

This week is a reminder that trading through a technical level is only the first step. What happens after the break matters.

Buyers moved above the moving averages but failed to clear the weekly high. Sellers broke below swing support but could not keep the price down. Both failures led to reversals.

Now bitcoin is back at the crossing. Get and stay above $82,500, and buyers have another opportunity to take control. Stay below, and sellers retain the advantage at resistance.

The levels define the risk. The follow-through will tell us who is taking control.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: USDCAD is lower on the day, but getting a modest lift after another higher inflation reading
item.description:
The USDCAD has seen plenty of up-and-down price action this week, but one message has been consistent: buyers have struggled to sustain momentum near the highs for the year.

The highs from October 5 and October 9 established a ceiling near 1.4292–1.4298. Monday’s high fell short at 1.4286. On Wednesday, the stronger-than-expected CPI data gave buyers another opportunity to push higher, but the rally stalled at 1.4298.

From there, the price rotated lower and closed back below the 100- and 200-hour moving averages near 1.4244.

Go figure. Stronger inflation. A lower USDCAD.

Yesterday’s higher-than-expected PPI data did not turn the tide either. Instead, the pair extended its decline, breaking below a key floor between 1.41922 and 1.4204.

Technical levels do matter. The buyers could not get through the ceiling. Once the moving averages and floor gave way, sellers had more control.

A longer-term support area gives buyers a place to lean

The selling continued today, taking the price into a swing area between 1.41297 and 1.4153.

That area supported the pair from mid-June into mid-July and also lines up with swing highs from November 2025. Today’s low reached 1.4146, putting the price inside that support zone.

The import/export price data provided another sign of inflation pressure—and another opportunity for traders to buy the US dollar.

Take a look at these concerns.

  • Fuel and lubricants: +34.5%. Natural gas rose 96.5%, although its small weight—roughly 0.3%—limits its overall influence.
  • Industrial supplies and materials: +20.4%.
  • Unfinished metals: +25.3%; finished metals: +18.5%.
  • Industrial supplies excluding fuels: +13.0%.
  • Nonelectrical machinery: +10.4%; capital goods: +8.4%.
  • Imports excluding food and fuels: +6.2%.

Food, autos and consumer goods are comparatively less troublesome: annual increases were 2.9%, 1.1% and 2.7%, respectively.

Import takeaway: The persistent concern is the cost of equipment and production inputs. Energy explains September’s biggest jump, but it does not explain away the broader inflation pressure.

The USD is finding a bid.  The difference this time?

Although the USD moved lower on the CPI and the PPI, today we are seeing a modest bid.  Why?  The USDCAD had already moved lower from its highs for the year and reached an established technical support area. Buyers now have a level against which to define their risk.

The question is whether they "can hold the support?".

A move back above 1.4153, followed by an ability to stay above it, would strengthen the case for a bounce. While the price remains inside the zone, buyers and sellers are still battling.

The lower boundary at 1.41297 is the key downside risk level. Stay above it, and buyers retain an opportunity to build a recovery. Move below it and stay below, and another layer of support gives way, opening the door for further selling.

What would a recovery need to clear?

On further upside momentum, the targets come in at:

  • 1.41922–1.4204: The broken floor. Prior support becomes potential resistance.

  • 1.4223: The falling 100-hour moving average.

  • 1.4233: The falling 200-hour moving average.

Holding support is a start. Getting back above those resistance levels would provide evidence that buyers are taking back control.

The trading lesson: Prepare before you trade

Hotter inflation data can give traders a reason to buy the dollar. It does not guarantee that the price will move higher—or stay higher.

This week, buyers had their opportunities near the highs and could not sustain the momentum. Today, they are trying again from a different technical location: support.

For traders, that creates a framework. Know where support is. Know what would invalidate the bounce. Know where the next resistance levels could stall a recovery.

In the video above, I detail the technical levels in play and show why they matter.

You need to prepare for your trade. Not just trade.

item.title: US September import price index +1.1% vs +0.8% expected
item.description:
• Prior was +0.7% m/m (revised to +0.5%)
  • Export prices +2.2% vs +1.0% expected
  • Prior export prices were +0.6% (revised to +1.2%)
  • Import prices y/y 8.1%  vs +7.0% prior

It's been an ugly week for inflation data. The market seems to think the Fed can tame it by waiting until December but that's some serious imported inflation that's going to be working its way through prices for awhile.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes the import and export price indexes  monthly. They measure what US buyers pay for foreign goods and services and what foreign buyers pay for American output. The data rarely moves markets on its own, but it is a useful read on how the dollar, global commodity prices and foreign producer costs are feeding into the US economy. One point worth knowing: import prices exclude tariffs and duties. That makes the series a clean test of whether foreign exporters are absorbing tariff costs or passing them through. It is also one of the inputs used to deflate trade in the GDP accounts.

In August, import prices rose 0.7%, and energy dominated. Import fuel prices were up 26.8% from a year earlier, and natural gas import prices more than doubled, rising 102.6%. Export prices climbed 8.6% over the 12 months to August. China stands out: import prices from China rose 1.0% in August, the biggest monthly gain since the series started in January 2004.

The September report follows two hot inflation prints this week. Headline CPI rose to 3.7% y/y against 3.6% expected, with core at 2.6% versus a 2.5% forecast and a 0.33% monthly gain. Energy jumped 5.2% on the month, and a 9.1% surge in gasoline accounted for more than half the overall increase. PPI was worse. Producer prices rose 1.3% m/m and 6.3% y/y, far above the consensus of 0.5% and 5.3%. That was the fastest monthly increase since March 2022 and the highest annual rate since December 2022.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

The US dollar continues its move to the downside today despite the hotter US CPI and PPI reports this week. Treasury yields are also higher this morning, but the greenback is struggling to attract buyers.

In the morning video above, I take a look at the three major currency pairs—EURUSD, USDJPY and GBPUSD—from a technical perspective. For each pair, I outline the bias, the risk-defining levels and the targets that would give either the buyers or sellers more control.

The disconnect between the inflation headlines and the dollar’s direction is worth watching. Stronger inflation would normally offer support through expectations for tighter monetary policy. However, traders still need to see that fundamental story reflected in the price action. This morning, the dollar is mostly moving the other way.

Dollar lower against six of seven major currencies

The dollar’s largest decline is against the NZD, followed by the AUD. USDJPY is the exception, holding a marginal gain on the day even after retreating from its highs earlier this week.

From the dollar’s perspective:

  • Against the NZD: down approximately 0.82%.

  • Against the AUD: down approximately 0.56%.

  • Against the CHF: down approximately 0.50%.

  • Against the GBP: down approximately 0.49%.

  • Against the EUR: down approximately 0.34%.

  • Against the CAD: down approximately 0.23%.

  • Against the JPY: up approximately 0.02%.

AUDUSD is trading near 0.6958, rebounding after the weaker Australian employment report and yesterday’s fall.

The recovery is a reminder that the initial reaction to an economic release is only part of the story. Sellers need follow-through to keep control. When that selling stalls and the price starts recovering, traders need to reassess their risk.

Ueda keeps the weak yen and inflation in focus

Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda is on the wires saying policymakers are watching the weak yen in terms of inflation.

His other remarks indicate that the timing and pace of future rate increases will depend on developments including foreign exchange, AI-related demand and the Middle East. He described economic and price developments as broadly consistent with the BOJ’s forecasts and reiterated that financial conditions remain accommodative.

A weaker yen can raise import costs and add to domestic price pressures. That keeps the currency relevant to the BOJ’s policy decisions—and keeps traders sensitive to comments about further tightening.

USDJPY falls below its converged hourly moving averages

USDJPY moved higher earlier this week but fell just short of the September 24 high.

The buyers had their shot. They could not get through that prior peak, and the subsequent retreat has taken the price back below the nearly converged 100- and 200-hour moving averages near 158.23.

With the pair trading around 158.01, that moving-average area becomes the close risk for sellers.

  • Stay below 158.23 is more bearish and keeps sellers in control against that area.

  • Move back above—and stay above—and the downside break loses some of its significance.

  • On the downside, today’s low near 157.80 is the first reference point. A break below would extend the session’s range and give sellers additional confirmation.

(see video)

When the 100- and 200-hour moving averages converge, they create a relatively clear decision area. Traders can lean against that area with risk defined and limited. The next move is uncertain, but the level that would weaken the trading idea is identifiable.

Currency ranges: USDJPY has the most room to extend

The session ranges compared with the displayed 22-day average ranges show different conditions across the three major pairs:

  • EURUSD: 1.1209 to 1.1269 — approximately 60 pips, or 92% of its 65-pip average range.

  • USDJPY: 157.80 to 158.18 — approximately 38 pips, or 38% of its 101-pip average range.

  • GBPUSD: 1.1268 to 1.1349 — approximately 81 pips, or 111% of its 73-pip average range.

USDJPY has covered the smallest share of its average range, leaving the most room to extend relative to recent trading conditions.

EURUSD has completed most of a typical day’s range, while GBPUSD has already exceeded its average. That does not mean either pair has to stop moving. The average is a guide to the day’s activity, not a ceiling.

US stock futures are mixed

US futures show modest weakness in the Dow, a small gain in the S&P and a larger decline in the Nasdaq:

  • Dow futures: down 10.69 points.

  • S&P 500 futures: up 8.4 points.

  • Nasdaq futures: down 96 points.

The mixed performance leaves technology shares lagging heading into the North American session.

Treasury yields move higher

US Treasury yields are higher, with the longer maturities showing the larger increases:

  • 2-year: 4.7571%, up 0.61 basis points.

  • 5-year: 4.9166%, up 1.96 basis points.

  • 10-year: 5.1103%, up 2.33 basis points.

  • 30-year: 5.4518%, up 2.38 basis points.

The 10-year yield is back above 5.10%, but the rise in yields has yet to translate into broad dollar strength this morning. Despite the stronger PPI yesterday, yields moved lower.  Go figure. 

European equities mostly higher

  • Germany’s DAX: 25,585.68, up 0.80%.

  • France’s CAC 40: 7,951.61, up 0.21%.

  • UK FTSE 100: 10,830.91, down 0.09%.

  • Spain’s IBEX 35: 19,318.91, up 0.74%.

  • Italy’s FTSE MIB: 49,732.12, up 0.34%.

Gold, silver and Bitcoin edge higher

Gold is trading near $4,177.92, up approximately 0.17%. Silver is near $57.80, up approximately 0.74%.

Bitcoin is trading near $82,656, up approximately 0.64%.

What is ahead in North American trading?

The US calendar brings another inflation reading, followed by an update on industrial activity:

  • 8:30 AM ET: September import prices.

  • 9:15 AM ET: September industrial production and capacity utilization. Industrial production is expected to rise 0.4%, following an unchanged reading in August.

Import prices add another piece to the inflation picture after this week’s CPI and PPI reports. Industrial production will help show whether activity is holding up alongside those price pressures.

For the dollar, the reaction matters. Stronger data needs to attract sustained buying to change the current direction.

EURUSD: Buyers push toward the session high

EURUSD is trading near 1.1256, toward the upper end of its range. The session high near 1.1269 is the immediate upside reference.

A break above that high would extend the recovery. If buyers cannot get through, the focus shifts to whether they can maintain control on a rotation lower. In the video, I outline the technical support levels that help define that risk.

GBPUSD: An above-average move higher

GBPUSD is trading near 1.1338, close to its session high at 1.1349.

The pair has already exceeded its average daily range. That gives context to the size of the move, but it does not provide a sell signal by itself. Sellers still need a technical reason to enter, and buyers need to hold support to maintain control.

In the video, I define those decision points for GBPUSD and EURUSD, along with the important 158.23 moving-average area in USDJPY.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: BOJ’s Ueda: We will continue to raise rates as underlying inflation approaches 2%
item.description:
• Want to gauge neutral rate estimate taking into account accumulative impact of past rate hikes on financial conditions, domestic prices
  • Hard to say anything clear about Japan’s neutral rate of interest
  • Takeaway from this week’s meetings was to exchange views with other policymakers on how Middle East conflict and AI demand could affect global, Japanese economies and inflation
  • As we have said, our policy has entered a new phase as underlying inflation is quite close to 2%, we cannot allow inflation to rise further
  • As underlying inflation is quite close to 2%, it is becoming more important than before to anchor inflation around our target
  • Haven’t been in touch with US Treasury Secretary Bessent since we met in Asheville
  • Timing, pace of future rate hikes will be decided looking at impact of FX, AI demand and Middle East developments on prices
  • We will discuss at upcoming meeting whether to tweak our assessment that underlying inflation is approaching 2%
  • Did not hear anything at this week’s meetings that deviated from our baseline view
  • Economic, price moves roughly in line with our forecasts
  • We will continue to raise interest rates as underlying inflation approaching 2%, financial conditions are accommodative
  • I felt that there were more policymakers at this meeting who were somewhat more bullish on AI demand than we had estimated
  • No big gap in view between what we have assessed on inflationary pressure from AI demand, and what I heard from global policymakers

Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda said at the IMF meetings that the BOJ will continue to raise interest rates, with underlying inflation approaching 2% and financial conditions still accommodative. The BOJ policy rate is currently at 1.25% and the market sees little chance of a hike at the October 30 meeting but that rises to 75% for the December 18 meeting.

Ueda said policy has entered a new phase and that the BOJ cannot allow inflation to rise further. With underlying inflation quite close to target, anchoring it around 2% is becoming more important than before. He said the BOJ will discuss at its upcoming meeting whether to tweak its assessment that underlying inflation is approaching 2%.

The timing and pace of future hikes will depend on the impact of FX, AI demand and Middle East developments on prices. Economic and price moves are roughly in line with BOJ forecasts, and he said nothing he heard at this week’s meetings deviated from the baseline view.

On AI, Ueda said more policymakers than expected were bullish on AI demand, but there was no big gap between the BOJ’s assessment of AI-driven inflation pressure and what he heard from global counterparts.

He said Japan’s neutral rate remains hard to pin down. Ueda exchanged views with Fed Chair Warsh but declined to comment on the discussion, and said he hasn’t been in touch with Treasury Secretary Bessent since they met in Asheville, which is notable on the intervention front.

USD/JPY is flat today at 158.00 while the US dollar is broadly weaker elsewhere.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: investingLive European session wrap: Dollar slips as stocks steady and yields edge a little higher
item.description:
Headlines:

  • Gold shrugs off hot inflation data as market focus may be shifting to growth concerns
  • How have interest rate expectations changed after this week's events?
  • Chart of the day: 10-year Treasury yields hit reverse this week but the real test is still ahead
  • Eurozone September final CPI +3.8% vs +3.8% y/y prelim

Markets:

  • NZD leads, USD and JPY lag on the day
  • 10-year Treasury yields up 2.5 bps to 5.11%
  • WTI crude oil -0.3% to $96.20
  • Gold up 0.2% to $4,176
  • European stocks higher; S&P 500 futures +0.1%
  • Bitcoin up 0.7% to $82,577

It was a quieter session as broader markets continue to digest the calmer mood as we look toward the final stages this week.

The selloff in the bond market had stalled in recent days despite hotter-than-expected US inflation data, helping investors to afford a breather. And that relief is continuing to today for the most part.

We are seeing 10-year Treasury yields nudge back up a little to 5.11% but so far, the broader market reaction is still siding with the calmer side. That as 10-year yields are still poised for back-to-back weekly declines for the first time since June.

The dollar is struggling once again as we get into the final stretch of the week, with EUR/USD up 0.3% to 1.1256 in hitting a one-week high. USD/JPY is slightly calmer as it keeps little changed near 158.00 but the dollar is faltering elsewhere with AUD/USD up 0.6% to 0.6960 and USD/CAD down 0.3% to 1.4147 on the day.

In the equities space, European stocks are building on the better mood still as regional indices are posting modest gains today. The DAX is up 0.9% with the CAC 40 up just 0.3% as French stocks are not as enthusiastic amid fiscal risks back home. Still, both indices are poised to post their fifth weekly gain in six weeks.

As for US futures, the mood music continues to be rather dour for tech shares. S&P 500 futures are up 0.1% but Nasdaq futures are down 0.2%, as the tech selloff looks to hold despite the late recovery yesterday.

In other markets, gold is up 0.2% to $4,176 as the precious metal sticks with the post-CPI rebound but is unable to breach key resistance closer to $4,200 still.

There won't be much on the agenda in the session ahead to shake things up, so broader markets will continue to be left to digest the inflation developments this week and weigh that against the "higher for longer" narrative as central bank decisions will slowly come back into focus in the coming weeks.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Ethereum rebounds as dip-buyers pile in around key technical levels. Fundamental improvement or just a dead-cat bounce?

The macro and geopolitical pictures haven’t improved at all, so the rebound looks to be driven more by overstretched positioning.

This could limit the upside unless we get a breakthrough in US-Iran negotiations or the economic data continues to point towards a strong economy while the Fed remains slow in addressing inflationary pressures.

Looking ahead, we have the Flash PMIs, the FOMC, US–Iran negotiations and the US midterm elections as key catalysts. Deteriorating economic data could increase concerns about growth, further weighing on risk sentiment and Ethereum.

What could change the picture completely would be an end to the US–Iran war, as that would ease inflationary pressures, improve the growth outlook and likely support a broader recovery in the crypto market.

item.title: Is EUR/USD finally turning the corner or is this just another false dawn?
item.description:
The past few weeks have been rather painful for EUR/USD buyers but it seems like things are finally taking a turn for the better. Ironically, this is all coming after hotter-than-expected US inflation data from the CPI and PPI reports this week. Yet, that is helping to give EUR/USD a lift as it pushes to 1.1260 today - the highest in a little over a week.

The immediate reaction to the US CPI report on Wednesday saw the pair fall to a low of 1.1114 before staging a meaningful rebound in the past few sessions. And with that, the technical picture is also starting to look more encouraging for buyers.

Of note, EUR/USD has managed to climb back above both its 100-hour (red line) and 200-hour (blue line) moving averages for the first time in five weeks. That marks a significant shift in near-term momentum, especially considering how the two key levels have repeatedly capped upside attempts throughout the recent decline.

But before getting too excited about a further run to the upside, there's still some work to be done.

For one, buyers are now contesting resistance from the 23.6 Fib retracement level of the swing lower from August to October, at around 1.1254. A firm break above that will then draw in the swing highs from earlier this month around 1.1275-80 next. And after that, there is the region around 1.1340-50 to tackle with the 38.2 Fib retracement level at 1.1341 sitting thereabouts.

The pair definitely does look like it wants to come up for some air, but there's plenty of technical hurdles to get through before convincing of a stronger shift in trading sentiment. As things stand, I'd argue that what we are seeing looks more like a breather for the euro rather than a decisive trend reversal.

And why is that you might ask? Well, it is all on the bond market.

The sharp retreat in Treasury yields from their recent highs has definitely helped to take some pressure off the pair as the dollar also slides back a little. But with 10-year yields still hovering above 5%, the underlying macro backdrop hasn't exactly changed. Inflation remains stubborn for the most part and another push higher in yields could easily spoil the recovery in EUR/USD.

Besides that, Europe isn't free of its own troubles either. The fiscal worries in France remain a lingering threat, particularly if the French-German yield spread starts widening again. It is keeping at around 138 bps today, not too far away from the 150 bps high from two weeks ago. If things heat up again, that could quickly put renewed pressure on the single currency.

Taking all of that into consideration, the charts appear to be giving the euro some breathing room to work with for the time being. But at the end of the day, the bond market is the one that will have the final say on whether the rebound can turn into something more constructive.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.
